Two-day meeting with unprecedented Day 1 dedicated entirely to zero-bound monetary policy tools and unconventional policy strategies — the first such internal seminar in FOMC history. Gramlich explicitly notes four simultaneous historically rare economic events (largest positive productivity shock since 1917, jobless recovery, inflation threatening to go below target, unprecedented public communication demands) interacting for the first time. Economy is accelerating (Q2 GDP 2.4% surprise) while simultaneously the Committee is introducing the most dovish forward guidance in its history — a unique combination.

Governor Fischer (new Board member) participates; raises question about PCE vs CPI target. First meeting where Yellen explicitly addresses taper endpoint (October vs. December) as a live question. Fisher proposes reinvestment tapering as pre-liftoff tool.

Two-day meeting (Mar 17-18). Day 1 focused on ON RRP/liftoff mechanics; Day 2 economic go-around and policy. 'Patient' dropped. One formal dissent (Kocherlakota, preferred Alt A). Strong consensus (9-1) for Alt B. Key headwinds: dollar +15%, energy prices, Q1 GDP weakness. Labor market near natural rate. Inflation well below target on transitory factors.

Two-day meeting (Apr 28-29). Day 1 covered balance sheet/reinvestment. Q1 GDP confirmed very weak (~0%). 'At least in part reflecting transitory factors' language debated. No formal dissents. June liftoff essentially removed; September emerging as base case. Kocherlakota-Evans dovish wing prominent (2016+ preferred). Bullard flagged financial stability. Greece escalating.

File begins directly with economic go-around (no Day 1 preamble). Q1 GDP weakness largely attributed to residual seasonality; Q2 rebound in progress. Unemployment stalled at 5.5%. ECI surprised upward but Rosengren flagged distortion. Greece at critical stage. September liftoff crystallizing as majority base case. No formal dissents. ~8 members lean hawkish vs. ~5 more cautious.

Two-day meeting (Jul 28-29). Day 1 covered balance sheet normalization + financial stability tabletop exercise. Economic go-around starts line 2029. Q2 GDP rebounding (~2%). Unemployment 5.3%; ECI 2.8% but Rosengren flagged geographic distortion. China stock market crash major new uncertainty. Greece mostly resolved. Oil fell 20% since June. Statement added 'some' in para 3. Kocherlakota formally dissented (preferred Alt A). September liftoff still majority base case. Evans, Brainard, Tarullo skeptical.

Two-day meeting (Sep 16-17). Day 1: balance sheet/reinvestment discussion. Day 2: hold decision (Alt B). Lacker formally dissented (preferred raise). Bullard and Williams expressed clear preference for Alt C (raise). August 24 China shock (Dow -1,000 at open; 1,200+ circuit breakers) major new event. Unemployment 5.1% = natural rate estimate. All wage acceleration (ECI) fully revised away. Dollar +15% from year ago. Brazil junk downgrade. China growth uncertainty elevated. Tarullo delivered extended speech on epistemological uncertainty about natural rate. Kocherlakota submitted negative rate as appropriate in SEP. Yellen recommended hold based on global risk asymmetry.

Two-day meeting. Day 1 was a dedicated r* seminar (not scored as economic go-round). Day 2 scoring represents the economic and policy go-rounds. Kocherlakota's extreme dovish views (last meeting before departure) are flagged as outlier — not allowed to dominate center-of-gravity. Meeting had notably dispersed views across hawks (Lacker, Williams), doves (Kocherlakota), and skeptics (Tarullo, Brainard).

Historic liftoff meeting — first rate increase since 2006. Near-unanimous vote to raise rates 25bp. Tarullo was the most skeptical participant but ultimately supported the decision; no formal dissents against the hike. Significant discussion of Third Avenue fund closure and high-yield market stress in the days before the meeting. Williams notable as SEP outlier (4-5 hikes in 2016 vs. median 3-4). Brainard most prominently dovish within the consensus, emphasizing inflation persistence and global risks.

Meeting held during significant financial market turbulence (China devaluation fears, oil crash to ~$30, VIX elevated, S&P down ~8% from December liftoff). Meeting opened with consensus statement discussion; Bullard formally dissented on "symmetric" language in the statement, not on the hold decision. This is the first post-liftoff hold meeting. The labor market/GDP divergence (strong payrolls vs. weak Q4 GDP ~1%) was a prominent puzzle discussed by multiple participants.

Meeting occurs in the aftermath of significant financial market turbulence (January–February 2016), with conditions having recovered substantially by meeting time. Core PCE jumped to 1.7% in January — the most significant inflation improvement in several years — but Tealbook projects reversal back to ~1.5%, creating uncertainty about persistence. Rosengren raises novel banking fragility concern (U.S. large bank stocks -25%, European banks -30% from December peak). Fischer explicitly keeps April and June as live meeting options. Brainard's endogeneity argument (financial conditions improvement is partly a function of reduced U.S. hike expectations) is a notable analytical dissent from the mainstream view.

Q1 GDP residual seasonality debate is prominent — Tealbook estimates ~0.5% but Williams and Lacker argue underlying ~2% after seasonal adjustment. This creates genuine uncertainty about OUTPUT_GAP scoring. Bullard proposes major reframing of FOMC messaging (drop dot plot forward guidance, say rates at "correct level," emphasize balanced risks, no forward guidance on direction) — a conceptual dissent that does not map cleanly onto the hawkish-dovish spectrum. Brexit (June 23 UK referendum) is a newly prominent risk explicitly discussed by Brainard, Fischer, and others. Near-consensus productivity pessimism — multiple speakers explicitly reject the Tealbook's assumption of productivity acceleration.

Day 1 of meeting devoted largely to long-run monetary policy framework/balance sheet operating regime discussion (not economic assessment). Economic go-around starts approximately line 1730 of transcript. Scoring based on economic go-around and policy discussion only.

Three formal dissents (Rosengren, George, Mester) — extremely rare; this meeting has one of the highest dissent counts in the modern FOMC era. DISSENT_INTENSITY scored near the top of the "significant division" range accordingly.

Meeting held one week before the U.S. presidential election; elevated election-related uncertainty affects several dimensions. First ~1380 lines of transcript cover balance sheet/operating framework discussion unrelated to economic assessment; scoring based on economic go-around (lines ~1980+) and policy discussion only.

Meeting occurs 5 weeks after the surprise election of Donald Trump; post-election market moves (10yr +60bp, equities at record highs, dollar +5%) and major fiscal policy uncertainty are the dominant themes. SEP dots shifted up to 3 hikes for 2017. UNCERTAINTY_EXPRESSED is simultaneously high alongside HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN — unusual combination explained by certainty about the December action but deep uncertainty about what post-election fiscal policy implies for 2017+.

Large portion of transcript (~30%) devoted to balance sheet/reinvestment policy discussion; this is categorized as policy planning, not financial conditions assessment. Financial stability emphasis score reflects only actual financial conditions discussion, not the balance sheet policy debate.

Morning CPI release on Day 2 (June 14) was incorporated in real time into statement language discussions; Yellen proposed adding "monitoring inflation developments closely" language during the policy go-round. This is an unusual intra-meeting data arrival that influenced the statement but not the SEP submissions.

Fischer's opening financial stability remarks use "flashing red" terminology for asset valuations — the first time in the history of the FOMC's quarterly stability assessment (QS) that asset prices reached the red category. This represents a notable escalation in financial stability language and anchors the above-average FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS score. Additionally, the meeting features an explicit reference to a staff memo commissioned to explain persistently low inflation, indicating unusually elevated model uncertainty.

Two-day meeting with an extensive special topic discussion on ELB/policy framework review that dominated Day 1 discussion. This is not a standard economic/policy go-round structure; the ELB discussion was forward-looking and strategic rather than about current conditions.
Day 1 dominated by operating framework discussion (floor vs. corridor system, policy rate choice). Economic and policy dimensions scored from the economic go-round and Day 2 policy go-round only.

Day 1 dominated by operating framework/balance sheet discussion (first ~920 lines). Sharp disconnect between strong economic data and deteriorating financial conditions/sentiment ("data good, mood bad"). Highest dissent intensity in this scoring series, with three participants explicitly favoring alt-A and several others expressing significant ambivalence about the hike.

Day 1 dominated by balance sheet framework discussion (floor system formalization, ample reserves language, plan for stopping runoff). Economic and policy dimensions scored from Day 2 go-rounds only. Government shutdown caused data gaps. Dramatic dovish pivot — removed "further gradual increases," added "patient." Most unified committee in recent period despite being at a major inflection point.

Day 1 dominated by extensive balance sheet normalization discussion (ending runoff September, taper debate, MBS reinvestment, portfolio composition). Day 2 included Thomas briefing on asymmetric loss function prompting extended u*/Phillips curve discussion. SEP meeting — median dots shifted to zero hikes in 2019. Multiple participants (Barkin, Bostic, Mester, George, Quarles, Brainard) explicitly argued for removing "patient" language soon. Notable increase in financial stability discussion (Kaplan on corporate debt, Brainard on CCyB/macroprudential).

Day 1 included extensive balance sheet composition discussion (SOMA maturity structure, transition speed). Day 2 featured Thomas briefing on 1994-95 soft landing episode, prompting extended discussion. Core PCE at 1.6% — lowest in the scoring window — dominates policy discussion. Bullard explicitly argues policy is "mildly restrictive" and rate cut may be warranted; Evans strongly supports. Staff revised underlying inflation down to flat 1.8% through 2021. The inflation miss is the pivotal development despite strong growth and labor market data.

First formal dissent in the scoring window (Bullard, in favor of 25bp cut). SEP nearly bimodal (8 for cuts, 9 flat) — highest internal division. Core PCE at 1.6% and inflation expectations at record lows — lowest inflation readings in window. Trade escalation (May 5 China + Mexico tariff threat) described as "game changer." Yield curve inverted. Removed "patient" language, replaced with "act as appropriate." Notable financial stability discussion — multiple participants cite corporate debt/asset valuation concerns as reason for caution on easing.

Very long meeting includes extensive framework review discussion (Day 1 morning) that is not about current economic conditions. Economic go-around and policy discussion are scored. Two formal dissents (Rosengren, George for no cut) plus strong reservations from Mester, Harker, Bostic, Barkin.

Meeting includes extensive framework review discussion (Day 1) and a notable repo market turmoil discussion on Day 2 before policy go-round. Saudi oil attack days before meeting adds new geopolitical risk. Three formal dissents for no cut (Rosengren, George — two voting dissenters; Harker, Mester, Bostic also prefer hold). Bullard dissents for 50bp cut.

This is an INTER-MEETING VIDEOCONFERENCE CALL, not a standard FOMC meeting. The entire call is devoted to operational/technical issues: rebuilding reserve balances after the September 2019 repo market turmoil, pace and composition of Treasury bill purchases, repo operations, communications strategy, and the longer-term question of a standing repo facility. There is ZERO discussion of macroeconomic conditions (inflation, output, labor, consumption, investment) and NO discussion of the stance of monetary policy (rate decisions). Most core dimensions are scored N/A due to truly zero discussion. Only FINANCIAL_TIGHTNESS, DISSENT_INTENSITY, FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS, and UNCERTAINTY_EXPRESSED are scored, and these reflect narrowly operational concerns rather than broad economic/policy assessments. Participants include: Powell, Williams, Rosengren, Harker, Quarles, Daly, Evans, Clarida, Kaplan, Barkin, Bullard, George, Bostic, Mester, Bowman, Kashkari, Brainard. Consensus: faster-paced Treasury bill purchases (~$60B/month) with announcement before the October FOMC meeting, to be decided by notation vote.

Third consecutive 25bp cut with signal of a pause. Statement language changed from "act as appropriate" to "continue to monitor the implications of incoming information for the economic outlook as it assesses the appropriate path." Six participants prefer hold (Rosengren, Harker, Mester, Bostic, Barkin, George) — the largest number of hold-supporters in the 2019 cutting cycle. Two formal voting dissents (Rosengren, George). Extensive financial stability discussion segment with multiple participants raising corporate debt, leveraged lending, declining bank capital buffers, and climate risk. Meeting also includes framework review discussion and standing repo facility discussion on Day 1. Q3 GDP released during the meeting at 1.9%.

First unanimous hold after three consecutive 25bp cuts. All 17 participants support Alt-B. Significant debate about statement language — "near" vs. "returning to" vs. "centered on" 2 percent — reflecting disagreement about whether current inflation (1.6%) is acceptable. Chair Powell declines to change language at this meeting. November jobs report was very strong (+266K). Framework review discussion continues on Day 1. Multiple participants discuss standing repo facility. Energy sector decline flagged (cap-ex expected down 15% in 2020). Brainard raises financial stability concerns about prolonged accommodation.

Day 1 framework review devoted to financial stability and inflation ranges — the most extensive financial stability discussion in the scoring sequence. Dedicated financial stability go-round on Day 1. Statement language changed from "near" to "returning to" 2 percent, explicitly acknowledging inflation shortfall. Kashkari prefers Alt-A but supports Alt-B. Coronavirus outbreak in Wuhan emerging as new risk but not yet dominant. Multiple participants advocate outcome-based forward guidance (hold until inflation at 2% sustainably). Rosengren delivers extensive warning about financial imbalances and "macroeconomic malpractice" of ignoring financial stability. Significant debate about inflation ranges (indifference vs. uncertainty vs. operational). 5bp technical adjustment to IOER and ON RRP rates.

EMERGENCY INTER-MEETING VIDEOCONFERENCE CALL — the first emergency 50bp cut since October 2008. Convened in response to rapid global spread of COVID-19 and sharp tightening of financial conditions (S&P down ~12% in preceding week, worst since 2008). Only 6 of ~17 participants speak (Powell, Bullard, Kashkari, Mester, Daly, Evans, Brainard). No economic go-around, no standard policy go-around. Most core dimensions have very limited evidence (Low confidence) or are N/A (LABOR_TIGHTNESS, FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS). Rate cut from 1.50-1.75% to 1.00-1.25%. Coordinated with G-7 statement and cuts by Australia and Canada. Kashkari explicitly warns Committee may return to the zero lower bound. Mester supports "somewhat reluctantly." Bullard warns about "Fed put" perception. Powell instructs participants to avoid signaling further action at the upcoming March 15-16 meeting.

Emergency meeting called Sunday March 15, 2020 in response to COVID-19 pandemic. Meeting held outside regular schedule; no SEP released. Policy discussion entirely dominated by crisis response: 100bp rate cut to zero lower bound, "at least" $500B Treasury and $200B MBS purchases announced, discount window restructured. Financial stability/market functioning explicitly declared "job one" by Chair Powell. Multiple participants explicitly invoke Knightian uncertainty and abandon standard forecasting models. Dissent on rate size (50bp vs 100bp) from ~5 members but all voted for package. LABOR_TIGHTNESS diverges from OUTPUT_GAP intentionally: labor market had not yet collapsed in hard data at the time of the meeting though mass layoffs were anticipated imminently. This is a genuine historical outlier meeting; extreme scores on multiple dimensions (FINANCIAL_STABILITY_EMPHASIS 93, UNCERTAINTY_EXPRESSED 92, HAWKISH_DOVISH_LEAN 5) are warranted by the text.

COVID-era emergency meeting during lockdowns. Economy in unprecedented shutdown. Discussion dominated by pandemic uncertainty. Extensive financial stability go-round. Two-day meeting with full go-rounds on both days.

COVID-era meeting. Day 1 focused heavily on toolkit discussion (forward guidance, LSAPs, yield curve control) rather than economic assessment. May employment surprise created unusual optimism-pessimism tension. First SEP since January 2020.

Meeting dominated by framework review discussion — adoption of revised Statement on Longer-Run Goals (average inflation targeting, employment shortfalls). Day 1 content is primarily framework review, not economic assessment. Economic go-round scores have lower confidence due to limited direct evidence in the available content. COVID-era meeting with surging cases in Sun Belt states.

First FOMC meeting implementing outcome-based forward guidance under revised framework (adopted August 2020). COVID-era meeting with economy recovering faster than expected but still far below pre-pandemic levels. Two participants (Rosengren, Bostic) prefer option C (delay enhanced guidance). Fiscal policy stalemate is a major concern. K-shaped recovery dynamics prominent. Meeting also marked by tributes to Thomas Laubach.

COVID-era meeting with second wave surging — record U.S. cases, European lockdowns resuming. Day 1 dominated by asset purchase policy discussion (transitioning from market-functioning to accommodation rationale) and dedicated financial stability go-round. Election occurred November 3, two days before Day 2. CARES Act expired with no replacement. K-shaped recovery dynamics prominent — goods booming, services depressed; advantaged vs. disadvantaged sectors. Climate risk discussed by multiple participants in financial stability context. Q3 GDP of 33% annualized created tension between strong backward-looking data and deteriorating near-term outlook.
